blocks.text: Bring the loop's controls together

When a sequence has a clear starting point, condition, and step, for brings those three parts together. In for (int i{0}; i<4; ++i), i is initialized once, i<4 is checked before each iteration, and ++i runs after each body execution that reaches its end normally. A false check ends the sequence.

The loop uses 0, 1, 2, and 3 and does not run the body at 4. The first semicolon separates initialization from the condition; the second separates the condition from the update. The condition does not mean 'how many times': it is an expression evaluated using the current state. Understanding these roles lets you build new loops instead of memorizing one line.

blocks.text: Include or exclude the endpoint

Changing < to <= changes which values satisfy the condition. To display 1 through 4 inclusive, use i<=4; to visit four positions starting at 0, use i<4. Both can perform four iterations, but they use different values. The number of items and their positions are not interchangeable.

Before writing a condition, list the values in a small example of the intended loop. Check the first value, the last one, and the one immediately after it. This reasoning catches off-by-one errors: a missing last value, an extra one, or a shifted start. When we study collection indices, distinguishing the item count from the last index will matter even more.

blocks.text: Different step sizes

The step does not have to be one. If i starts at 1 and increases by 2, the values are 1, 3, 5, and so on. A limit can become false without the counter ever equaling the endpoint. Therefore, checking whether the counter remains below or above a boundary usually describes a loop better than requiring exact equality with a number the step might skip.

In a countdown, the step and comparison must work together. Subtracting one while the condition requires i>=2 leaves i at 1 when the loop ends. Increasing i under the same condition does not bring it closer to the exit. Choosing for does not, by itself, correct the wrong direction.

blocks.text: Control state and scope

A counter declared in the for header belongs to that structure and its body. It cannot be used by that name afterward. If we need to inspect the final state outside, we can declare the counter before the loop and use it in the header. This is a choice about scope and usage, not just how the code looks.

A simple loop is easier to read if its update happens in one place. Adding another ++i inside the body while keeping the one in the header advances twice per iteration. If we want steps of two, writing i+=2 in the header communicates that intention clearly. Do not mistake a readability recommendation for a language restriction.

Reviewing the loop header
The construction starts at 2, uses the condition i<5, and updates with ++i. The body runs with 2, 3, and 4. The value 5 appears only in the check that ends the loop; it is not printed by the body.
Compare the lab solution

Compare your version after converting the loop. Criteria: display Station 1 through Station 4, one line per workstation, without visiting 0 or 5. With while, you must explicitly preserve initialization, the check before the body, and the update after printing.

The first false condition checks i=5. Here i was declared before while and remains in that scope; in the original for loop, it belongs to the header's scope. The two programs are equivalent in the lines they print, even though the name's later availability differs. Moving ++i before printing changes the workstations shown.
